claim: The D. melanogaster strain DGRP_360 was generated by 20 generations of strict full-sib mating from an isofemale line derived from the Raleigh, NC USA population.
source: The D. melanogaster strain DGRP_360 was generated by 20 generations of strict full-sib mating from an isofemale line derived from the Raleigh, NC USA population (Mackay et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Mackay et al., 2012

claim: DGRP_360 was divided into 25 replicate sublines, each maintained at a census population size of 10 virgin females and 10 males per generation.
source: We divided DGRP_360 into 25 replicate sublines, each maintained at a census population size of 10 virgin females and 10 males per generation.
evidence: Describes the experimental design and procedures performed

claim: A total of 1,456 mutations were detected that were either fixed or segregating at high frequency (>0.20) on the euchromatic nuclear genome in the MA lines.
source: We detected a total of 1,456 mutations that were either fixed or segregating at high frequency (>0.20) on the euchromatic nuclear genome in the MA lines.
evidence: Direct observation from sequencing data analysis

claim: The number of mutations per MA line ranged from 35 to 193, with a mean of 63.
source: The number of mutations per MA line ranged from 35 to 193, with a mean of 63 (Supplementary file 1B).
evidence: Statistical summary of observed mutation counts

claim: The observed fixation probabilities of putative mutations agreed well with the expected probabilities given their initial frequencies at G60.
source: The observed fixation probabilities of putative mutations agreed well with the expected probabilities given their initial frequencies at G60 (Figure 2), suggesting that both the mutations and their frequency estimates were accurate.
evidence: Comparison between observed and expected fixation probabilities shown in Figure 2

claim: Among the 1456 mutations, there were 1203 single base substitutions (SBS), 17 multiple base substitutions (MBS), 141 deletions, 47 insertions, and 48 complex mutational events.
source: Among the 1456 mutations, there were 1203 single base substitutions (SBS), 17 multiple base substitutions (MBS), 141 deletions, 47 insertions, and 48 complex mutational events that involved a combination of base substitutions and indels (Supplementary file 1B).
evidence: Classification of detected mutations from sequencing data

claim: The indel mutation rate was approximately 1/6 that of single base substitutions.
source: The numbers of different types of mutations are proportional to their mutation rates; thus the indel mutation rate was approximately 1/6 that of SBS, and deletions occurred at a frequency three times higher than insertions.
evidence: Inference from observed mutation counts

claim: Deletions occurred at a frequency three times higher than insertions.
source: The numbers of different types of mutations are proportional to their mutation rates; thus the indel mutation rate was approximately 1/6 that of SBS, and deletions occurred at a frequency three times higher than insertions.
evidence: Inference from observed mutation counts (141 deletions vs 47 insertions)

claim: Of the 1203 single base substitutions, 595 were transitions and 608 were transversions, corresponding to a Ti/Tv ratio of 1.96.
source: Of the 1203 SBS, 595 were transitions (Ti) and 608 were transversions (Tv), corresponding to a Ti/Tv ratio of 1.96 (Figure 3).
evidence: Direct count from sequencing data shown in Figure 3

claim: There were twice as many base substitution mutations at G or C sites than at A or T sites.
source: There were twice as many base substitution mutations at G or C sites (n = 828) than at A or T sites (n = 401), which, given the 42.48% genomic GC content, indicated a strong bias (~ 2.80 fold increase) towards mutations at G or C bases.
evidence: Direct count from sequencing data

claim: Given the 42.48% genomic GC content, there is a strong bias (~2.80 fold increase) towards mutations at G or C bases.
source: There were twice as many base substitution mutations at G or C sites (n = 828) than at A or T sites (n = 401), which, given the 42.48% genomic GC content, indicated a strong bias (~ 2.80 fold increase) towards mutations at G or C bases.
evidence: Calculation based on observed mutation counts and genomic GC content

claim: A previous study using the same sequencing strategy of three D. melanogaster MA lines reported a Ti/Tv ratio of 1.95 and an approximately two-fold increase in mutations at G/C bases.
source: These numbers agreed well with a previous study using the same sequencing strategy of three D. melanogaster MA lines, which reported a Ti/Tv ratio of 1.95 and an approximately two-fold increase in mutations at G/C bases (Keightley et al., 2009).
evidence: Comparison to published results from Keightley et al., 2009

claim: There was no appreciable difference in local sequence (20 bp up and downstream) GC content between mutations and randomly sampled sites.
source: While there was no appreciable difference in local sequence (20 bp up and downstream) GC content between mutations and randomly sampled sites, indels appeared to occur more often in low complexity regions, where homopolymers and short tandem repeats can often be found and are prone to replication slippage (Figure 4).
evidence: Analysis of sequence context shown in Figure 4

claim: Indels appeared to occur more often in low complexity regions, where homopolymers and short tandem repeats can often be found and are prone to replication slippage.
source: While there was no appreciable difference in local sequence (20 bp up and downstream) GC content between mutations and randomly sampled sites, indels appeared to occur more often in low complexity regions, where homopolymers and short tandem repeats can often be found and are prone to replication slippage (Figure 4).
evidence: Analysis of sequence complexity shown in Figure 4

claim: Standing variation in the DGRP reflects the demographic history of the natural Raleigh, NC population and is depleted of exonic variants.
source: Standing variation in the DGRP reflects the demographic history of the natural Raleigh, NC population and is depleted of exonic variants (Figure 5a).
evidence: Analysis of genomic location distribution shown in Figure 5a

claim: The extent of depletion of exonic spontaneous mutations was much weaker than standing variation in the DGRP.
source: However, the extent of depletion of exonic spontaneous mutations was much weaker – the spectrum of spontaneous mutations detected in the MA lines more closely reflected the proportion of exonic, intronic and intergenic bases in the genome (Figure 5a).
evidence: Comparison of mutation distribution to genomic proportions shown in Figure 5a

claim: The spectrum of spontaneous mutations detected in the MA lines more closely reflected the proportion of exonic, intronic and intergenic bases in the genome.
source: However, the extent of depletion of exonic spontaneous mutations was much weaker – the spectrum of spontaneous mutations detected in the MA lines more closely reflected the proportion of exonic, intronic and intergenic bases in the genome (Figure 5a).
evidence: Comparison shown in Figure 5a

claim: The proportions of frame-shift, stop gained or lost, and nonsynonymous spontaneous mutations were significantly greater than the proportion of segregating polymorphisms in the DGRP for these categories.
source: Remarkably, the proportions of frame-shift, stop gained or lost, and nonsynonymous spontaneous mutations were significantly greater than the proportion of segregating polymorphisms in the DGRP for these categories (Figure 5b).
evidence: Comparison of functional impact distributions shown in Figure 5b

claim: Deleterious mutations that would otherwise be lost have accumulated in the MA lines.
source: While the fitness effects of these protein sequence mutations may differ under laboratory and natural environments, these results clearly indicate that deleterious mutations that would otherwise be lost have accumulated in the MA lines.
evidence: Inference from the enrichment of high-impact mutations in MA lines compared to DGRP

claim: The numbers of mutations per gene was primarily a function of gene length.
source: In keeping with the inference that spontaneous mutations accumulated under minimal natural selection, the numbers of mutations per gene was primarily a function of gene length (Figure 6); and there was no gene ontology (GO) category enrichment for genes harboring new mutations (Supplementary file 1C).
evidence: Relationship shown in Figure 6

claim: There was no gene ontology (GO) category enrichment for genes harboring new mutations.
source: In keeping with the inference that spontaneous mutations accumulated under minimal natural selection, the numbers of mutations per gene was primarily a function of gene length (Figure 6); and there was no gene ontology (GO) category enrichment for genes harboring new mutations (Supplementary file 1C).
evidence: GO enrichment analysis results

claim: The effective population size was estimated to be 2Ne=19 for the X chromosome and 2Ne=23 for autosomes.
source: Although the census population size of each MA line was 2Ne=40 haploid genomes, the effective population size was estimated to be 2Ne=19 for the X chromosome and 2Ne=23 for autosomes (Figure 7a,b).
evidence: Maximum likelihood estimation based on mutation frequency spectrum shown in Figure 7a,b

claim: The census population size of each MA line was 2Ne=40 haploid genomes.
source: Although the census population size of each MA line was 2Ne=40 haploid genomes, the effective population size was estimated to be 2Ne=19 for the X chromosome and 2Ne=23 for autosomes (Figure 7a,b).
evidence: Experimental design specification

claim: The frequency spectrum of the observed effective population size visually agreed with the expectation.
source: The frequency spectrum of the observed effective population size visually agreed with the expectation (Figure 7a,b).
evidence: Visual comparison shown in Figure 7a,b

claim: At the estimated effective population size, for selection coefficients s ranging between -0.01 and 0.01 and assuming additivity, the fixation probability is between 0.034 and 0.054.
source: At this population size, for selection coefficients s ranging between -0.01 and 0.01 and assuming additivity, the fixation probability u=1−e−2s1−e−4sNe (Kimura, 1957) is between 0.034 and 0.054, which closely centers around the fixation probability for neutral sites.
evidence: Calculation using Kimura's formula from Kimura, 1957

claim: The large difference between census and effective population sizes could be due to the large variance in number of offspring commonly observed in flies.
source: The large difference between census and effective population sizes could be due to the large variance in number of offspring commonly observed in flies (Crow and Morton, 1955).
evidence: Explanation supported by citation to Crow and Morton, 1955

claim: The X to autosome Ne ratio was slightly higher than the expected 0.75, but this difference was not statistically significant (P = 0.40).
source: Although the X to autosome Ne ratio was slightly higher than the expected 0.75, this difference was not statistically significant (P = 0.40).
evidence: Statistical test result

claim: The estimates of Ne did not differ whether or not presumably non-neutral mutations (mutations that changed amino acids) were included.
source: The estimates of Ne did not differ whether or not presumably non-neutral mutations (mutations that changed amino acids) were included, further suggesting that drift was the primary force driving mutation frequency dynamics in these MA lines.
evidence: Comparison of Ne estimates with and without nonsynonymous mutations

claim: Drift was the primary force driving mutation frequency dynamics in the MA lines.
source: The estimates of Ne did not differ whether or not presumably non-neutral mutations (mutations that changed amino acids) were included, further suggesting that drift was the primary force driving mutation frequency dynamics in these MA lines.
evidence: Inference from the lack of difference in Ne estimates with/without nonsynonymous mutations

claim: Given the estimated effective population size, the marginal probability of a mutation to attain the frequency cutoff (0.2) was 7.20% on the X chromosome and 6.18% on autosomes.
source: Given the estimated effective population size, the marginal (integrated over 60 generations) probability of a mutation to attain the frequency cutoff (0.2) was 7.20% on the X chromosome and 6.18% on autosomes.
evidence: Calculation based on simulation results

claim: The median spontaneous mutation rate was 5.21 × 10–9 per base on autosomes and 5.07 × 10–9 on the X chromosome for single base substitutions.
source: The median spontaneous mutation rate was 5.21 × 10–9 per base on autosomes and 5.07 × 10–9 on the X chromosome for single base substitutions and 0.79 × 10–9 on autosomes and 0.65 × 10–9 on the X chromosome for indels.
evidence: Calculated from observed mutations and estimated Ne

claim: The median spontaneous mutation rate was 0.79 × 10–9 on autosomes and 0.65 × 10–9 on the X chromosome for indels.
source: The median spontaneous mutation rate was 5.21 × 10–9 per base on autosomes and 5.07 × 10–9 on the X chromosome for single base substitutions and 0.79 × 10–9 on autosomes and 0.65 × 10–9 on the X chromosome for indels.
evidence: Calculated from observed mutations and estimated Ne

claim: The overall spontaneous mutation rate for all types of mutations combined was 6.25 × 10–9 on autosomes and 6.96 × 10–9 on the X chromosome.
source: The overall spontaneous mutation rate for all types of mutations combined was 6.25 × 10–9 on autosomes and 6.96 × 10–9 on the X chromosome (Figure 7c), similar to recent mutation rate estimates from MA studies using high throughput sequencing (Keightley et al., 2009; Schrider et al., 2013).
evidence: Calculated from observed mutations and estimated Ne, shown in Figure 7c

claim: The overall spontaneous mutation rate is similar to recent mutation rate estimates from MA studies using high throughput sequencing.
source: The overall spontaneous mutation rate for all types of mutations combined was 6.25 × 10–9 on autosomes and 6.96 × 10–9 on the X chromosome (Figure 7c), similar to recent mutation rate estimates from MA studies using high throughput sequencing (Keightley et al., 2009; Schrider et al., 2013).
evidence: Comparison to published mutation rates from Keightley et al., 2009 and Schrider et al., 2013

claim: There was substantial variation in spontaneous mutation rates among the MA lines.
source: There was substantial variation in spontaneous mutation rates among the MA lines (Figure 7c).
evidence: Variation shown in Figure 7c

claim: The mutation rate in MA19 was nearly a magnitude greater than the lines with the smallest mutation rates (MA08 for autosomes and MA15 for the X chromosome).
source: The mutation rate in MA19 was nearly a magnitude greater than the lines with the smallest mutation rates (MA08 for autosomes and MA15 for the X chromosome).
evidence: Comparison of mutation rates across lines

claim: The mutation rates on autosomes and the X chromosome showed no systematic difference (paired Wilcoxon rank sum test P = 0.64).
source: The mutation rates on autosomes and the X chromosome showed no systematic difference (Figure 7c, paired Wilcoxon rank sum test P = 0.64) and were positively correlated (Figure 7d), further suggesting the random distribution of mutations.
evidence: Statistical test result shown in Figure 7c

claim: The mutation rates on autosomes and the X chromosome were positively correlated.
source: The mutation rates on autosomes and the X chromosome showed no systematic difference (Figure 7c, paired Wilcoxon rank sum test P = 0.64) and were positively correlated (Figure 7d), further suggesting the random distribution of mutations.
evidence: Correlation shown in Figure 7d

claim: All organismal phenotypes accumulated significant between-line variance.
source: Although any pair of MA lines only differ on average by 126 sites, all organismal phenotypes and the expression of a large fraction of genes in both sexes (1526/7566 = 20.2% of expressed genes in females and 3,872/8,136 = 47.6% in males) accumulated significant between-line variance (Supplementary file 1D–E, Figure 8).
evidence: Statistical analysis of phenotypic variance

claim: The expression of 20.2% of expressed genes in females accumulated significant between-line variance.
source: Although any pair of MA lines only differ on average by 126 sites, all organismal phenotypes and the expression of a large fraction of genes in both sexes (1526/7566 = 20.2% of expressed genes in females and 3,872/8,136 = 47.6% in males) accumulated significant between-line variance (Supplementary file 1D–E, Figure 8).
evidence: Statistical analysis of gene expression variance

claim: The expression of 47.6% of expressed genes in males accumulated significant between-line variance.
source: Although any pair of MA lines only differ on average by 126 sites, all organismal phenotypes and the expression of a large fraction of genes in both sexes (1526/7566 = 20.2% of expressed genes in females and 3,872/8,136 = 47.6% in males) accumulated significant between-line variance (Supplementary file 1D–E, Figure 8).
evidence: Statistical analysis of gene expression variance

claim: Mutational heritability had a median of 0.55 x 10–3 for gene expression traits in females and 0.75 x 10–3 in males.
source: Mutational variance (Vm), the amount of genetic variation introduced by mutations in each generation, scaled by environmental variance and expressed as the mutational heritability (hm2= Vm/Ve), had a median of 0.55 x 10–3 for gene expression traits in females and 0.75 x 10–3 in males (Figure 8).
evidence: Calculated from variance components shown in Figure 8

claim: Mutational heritability for organismal traits ranged between 0.30 x 10–3 and 2.88 x 10–3.
source: hm2 for organismal traits ranged between 0.30 x 10–3 and 2.88 x 10–3, of the same order of magnitude as observed in earlier studies (Houle et al., 1996).
evidence: Calculated from variance components

claim: Mutational heritability for organismal traits is of the same order of magnitude as observed in earlier studies.
source: hm2 for organismal traits ranged between 0.30 x 10–3 and 2.88 x 10–3, of the same order of magnitude as observed in earlier studies (Houle et al., 1996).
evidence: Comparison to published results from Houle et al., 1996

claim: The difference in mutational heritabilities between gene expression traits and organismal phenotypes may be due to a larger number of QTLs influencing organismal traits and thus a larger mutational target size.
source: The difference in mutational heritabilities between gene expression traits and organismal phenotypes may be due to a larger number of QTLs influencing organismal traits and thus a larger mutational target size.
evidence: Speculative explanation for observed differences

claim: The rate of accumulation of genetic variation was significantly different for genes within many GO terms than the rest of the transcriptome.
source: Although mutations occurred randomly across the genome and were not associated with GO categories, the rate of accumulation of genetic variation was significantly different for genes within many GO terms than the rest of the transcriptome (Supplementary file 1F).
evidence: GO enrichment analysis of mutational variance

claim: In both sexes, mutational variance accumulated faster for genes involved in chitin metabolism, iron binding, and sensory perception of chemical stimulus.
source: For example, in both sexes, mutational variance accumulated faster for genes involved in chitin metabolism, iron binding, and sensory perception of chemical stimulus, but slower for genes involved in protein translation, mRNA splicing, and mitotic spindle organization.
evidence: GO enrichment analysis results

claim: In both sexes, mutational variance accumulated slower for genes involved in protein translation, mRNA splicing, and mitotic spindle organization.
source: For example, in both sexes, mutational variance accumulated faster for genes involved in chitin metabolism, iron binding, and sensory perception of chemical stimulus, but slower for genes involved in protein translation, mRNA splicing, and mitotic spindle organization.
evidence: GO enrichment analysis results

claim: Genes that are more plastic to macro-environmental perturbations accumulated genetic variation at a faster rate.
source: We observed that genes that are more plastic to macro-environmental perturbations accumulated genetic variation at a faster rate (Figure 9), suggesting a shared control of gene expression variation by mutations and environmental perturbations (Landry et al., 2007).
evidence: Correlation analysis shown in Figure 9

claim: There is a shared control of gene expression variation by mutations and environmental perturbations.
source: We observed that genes that are more plastic to macro-environmental perturbations accumulated genetic variation at a faster rate (Figure 9), suggesting a shared control of gene expression variation by mutations and environmental perturbations (Landry et al., 2007).
evidence: Inference from correlation between mutational variance and environmental plasticity, supported by citation to Landry et al., 2007

claim: Under the neutral model of polygenic phenotypic evolution, the among-line variance (Vg) in the DGRP inbred lines is 4NVm, where N is the effective size of the wild population from which DGRP was derived.
source: Under the neutral model of polygenic phenotypic evolution, the among-line variance (Vg) in the DGRP inbred lines is 4NVm, where N is the effective size of the wild population from which DGRP was derived (Lynch and Hill, 1986).
evidence: Theoretical expectation from Lynch and Hill, 1986

claim: The genome-wide nucleotide diversity in the DGRP (π) was estimated to be π = 4.92 x 10–3.
source: We estimated the genome-wide nucleotide diversity in the DGRP (π) to be π = 4.92 x 10–3 in the DGRP (Huang et al., 2014), from which we estimated N to be 186,363 (π4μ).
evidence: Calculated from DGRP sequence data from Huang et al., 2014

claim: The effective population size N of the wild Raleigh population was estimated to be 186,363.
source: We estimated the genome-wide nucleotide diversity in the DGRP (π) to be π = 4.92 x 10–3 in the DGRP (Huang et al., 2014), from which we estimated N to be 186,363 (π4μ).
evidence: Calculated from nucleotide diversity and mutation rate

claim: For all organismal and the majority of gene expression traits, the magnitude of standing genetic variation in the DGRP was much smaller than that predicted under the assumption of neutrality.
source: For all organismal and the majority of gene expression traits, the magnitude of standing genetic variation in the DGRP was much smaller than that predicted under the assumption of neutrality (Figure 10).
evidence: Comparison of observed Vg to neutral expectation shown in Figure 10

claim: There must be strong stabilizing selection that acts either directly on the traits (direct stabilizing selection) or through pleiotropic fitness effects of new mutations (apparent stabilizing selection).
source: Therefore, there must be strong stabilizing selection that acts either directly on the traits (direct stabilizing selection) or through pleiotropic fitness effects of new mutations (apparent stabilizing selection), which constrains the accumulation of genetic variation by mutations for gene expression and organismal traits (Denver et al., 2005; Rifkin et al., 2005).
evidence: Inference from the discrepancy between observed and neutral expectations, supported by citations to Denver et al., 2005 and Rifkin et al., 2005

claim: For the majority of traits, the ratio of mutational to standing genetic variance, Vm/Vg, far exceeded the expectation given the observed sequence variation.
source: For the majority of traits, the ratio of mutational to standing genetic variance, Vm/Vg, far exceeded the expectation given the observed sequence variation (Figure 10); thus the allelic effects of spontaneous mutations, E(am2), were several orders of magnitude larger than that of standing DNA variation, E(ag2).
evidence: Comparison shown in Figure 10

claim: The allelic effects of spontaneous mutations, E(am2), were several orders of magnitude larger than that of standing DNA variation, E(ag2).
source: For the majority of traits, the ratio of mutational to standing genetic variance, Vm/Vg, far exceeded the expectation given the observed sequence variation (Figure 10); thus the allelic effects of spontaneous mutations, E(am2), were several orders of magnitude larger than that of standing DNA variation, E(ag2).
evidence: Inference from the ratio of Vm/Vg exceeding sequence-based expectations

claim: The apparent stabilizing selection had either eliminated mutations with large effects on quantitative traits or modified their effects.
source: This result suggests that the apparent stabilizing selection, directly for fitness and indirectly for traits correlated with fitness, had either eliminated mutations with large effects on quantitative traits or modified their effects.
evidence: Inference from the difference in allelic effects between mutations and standing variation

claim: Genes expressed in both sexes are under slightly stronger selection than those expressed in only one sex.
source: First, genes expressed in both sexes are under slightly stronger selection than those expressed in only one sex, and the strength of selection has a modest but highly significant positive correlation between the two sexes (Figure 11).
evidence: Comparison of Vm/Vg for sex-specific vs non-specific genes shown in Figure 11

claim: The strength of selection has a modest but highly significant positive correlation between the two sexes.
source: First, genes expressed in both sexes are under slightly stronger selection than those expressed in only one sex, and the strength of selection has a modest but highly significant positive correlation between the two sexes (Figure 11).
evidence: Correlation analysis shown in Figure 11

claim: There is stronger selection for genes on the X chromosome than autosomal genes, and this effect is more pronounced in males than females.
source: Second, there is stronger selection for genes on the X chromosome than autosomal genes, and this effect is more pronounced in males than females (Figure 12).
evidence: Comparison of Vm/Vg by chromosome shown in Figure 12

claim: Many genes in GO categories associated with essential cellular functions related to transcription, translation, cell cycle, and energy metabolism appeared to be under stronger selection in both sexes.
source: Many genes in GO categories associated with essential cellular functions related to transcription, translation, cell cycle, and energy metabolism, among others, appeared to be under stronger selection in both sexes (Supplementary file 1G, Figure 13).
evidence: GO enrichment analysis of Vm/Vg shown in Figure 13

claim: The data unequivocally reject the neutral mutation – random drift balance model for maintenance of quantitative genetic variation.
source: Our data unequivocally reject the neutral mutation – random drift balance model for maintenance of quantitative genetic variation (Lynch and Hill, 1986).
evidence: Inference from comparison of observed Vg to neutral expectations

claim: The observed magnitude of segregating variation is much less than predicted under the neutral model given the estimates of population size in nature and mutational variation.
source: The observed magnitude of segregating variation is much less than predicted under this model given our estimates of population size in nature and mutational variation.
evidence: Comparison of observed Vg to neutral expectation 4NVm

claim: A form of stabilizing selection on a large fraction of gene expression as well as organismal traits constrains naturally occurring genetic variation.
source: Therefore, we inferred that a form of stabilizing selection on a large fraction of gene expression as well as organismal traits constrains naturally occurring genetic variation, consistent with earlier studies using a similar analysis in C. elegans (Denver et al., 2005) and inter-specific variation in Drosophila (Rifkin et al., 2005).
evidence: Inference from comparison of Vm and Vg, supported by citations to Denver et al., 2005 and Rifkin et al., 2005

claim: The apparent stabilizing selection detected is too weak by an order of magnitude for the majority of genes and quantitative traits to be consistent with observed selection against heterozygous effects of new mutations.
source: Thus, while we detect apparent stabilizing selection on quantitative traits, it is too weak by an order of magnitude for the majority of genes and quantitative traits to be consistent with observed selection against heterozygous effects of new mutations (Mukai et al., 1972; Mackay et al., 1992).
evidence: Comparison of estimated s to published selection coefficients from Mukai et al., 1972 and Mackay et al., 1992

claim: The rate of generation of new mutations is too weak a force to counter strong apparent stabilizing selection, which removes variation faster than it is generated.
source: Alternatively, the rate of generation of new mutations is too weak a force to counter strong apparent stabilizing selection, which removes variation faster than it is generated.
evidence: Alternative explanation for observed Vm/Vg ratios

claim: It is possible that stabilizing selection in nature is weaker than assumed.
source: It is possible that stabilizing selection in nature is weaker than assumed (Kingsolver et al., 2001; Kingsolver and Diamond, 2011), and other mechanisms such as balancing selection, fluctuating allelic effects in the face of temporally and spatially varying environments, canalization of mutational effects, and a combination of direct and apparent stabilizing selection all contribute (Barton, 1990; Zhang et al., 2002; Turelli and Barton, 2004; Zhang and Hill, 2005).
evidence: Speculative explanation supported by multiple citations

claim: Other mechanisms such as balancing selection, fluctuating allelic effects in the face of temporally and spatially varying environments, canalization of mutational effects, and a combination of direct and apparent stabilizing selection may all contribute to maintaining genetic variation.
source: It is possible that stabilizing selection in nature is weaker than assumed (Kingsolver et al., 2001; Kingsolver and Diamond, 2011), and other mechanisms such as balancing selection, fluctuating allelic effects in the face of temporally and spatially varying environments, canalization of mutational effects, and a combination of direct and apparent stabilizing selection all contribute (Barton, 1990; Zhang et al., 2002; Turelli and Barton, 2004; Zhang and Hill, 2005).
evidence: Speculative explanation supported by multiple citations

claim: Artificially introducing individual mutations or combinations of mutations and assessing their effects will be needed to understand the balance between mutations and selection in maintaining segregating genetic variation for quantitative traits.
source: Ultimately, artificially introducing individual mutations or combinations of mutations and assessing their effects, which is now feasible, will be needed to understand the balance between mutations and selection in maintaining segregating genetic variation for quantitative traits.
evidence: Proposed future experimental approach

claim: 51 mutations detected at G60 in MA lines 2, 11, 13, 17, or 24 were randomly selected and sequenced by Sanger sequencing at G130.
source: To validate mutations, we sequenced PCR fragments flanking 51 randomly selected mutations in pooled DNA from five MA lines (MA02, MA11, MA13, MA17, and MA24) in G130 using Sanger sequencing.
evidence: Description of validation experiment

claim: Mutations occurred randomly across the genome and were not associated with GO categories.
source: Although mutations occurred randomly across the genome and were not associated with GO categories, the rate of accumulation of genetic variation was significantly different for genes within many GO terms than the rest of the transcriptome (Supplementary file 1F).
evidence: GO enrichment analysis of mutation locations

claim: The MA lines accumulated a broad functional spectrum of spontaneous mutations, including a significant fraction of high impact mutations that would otherwise likely be removed by natural selection.
source: The MA lines accumulated a broad functional spectrum of spontaneous mutations, including a significant fraction of high impact mutations that would otherwise likely be removed by natural selection.
evidence: Summary of functional annotation results from Figure 5

claim: The relatively small number of mutations and the large number of genes with significant mutational variance in expression implies pervasive pleiotropic effects by new mutations.
source: The relatively small number of mutations and the large number of genes with significant mutational variance in expression implies pervasive pleiotropic effects by new mutations.
evidence: Inference from the discrepancy between number of mutations and number of genes with expression variance

claim: Gene expression traits often form co-expression modules.
source: Gene expression traits often form co-expression modules (Ayroles et al., 2009), and therefore mutations that directly influence expression of a small number of loci can cause secondary trans effects at a much larger number of genes.
evidence: Established knowledge supported by citation to Ayroles et al., 2009

claim: Mutations that directly influence expression of a small number of loci can cause secondary trans effects at a much larger number of genes.
source: Gene expression traits often form co-expression modules (Ayroles et al., 2009), and therefore mutations that directly influence expression of a small number of loci can cause secondary trans effects at a much larger number of genes.
evidence: Inference from co-expression module structure

claim: Selection will not act on individual traits, but rather on the combined effects of all traits.
source: Taking this networked view of gene expression traits, any selection will not act on individual traits, but rather on the combined effects of all traits.
evidence: Inference from the networked nature of gene expression

claim: There is stronger selection on genes that would cause trans pleiotropic effects such as transcription factors.
source: Consistent with this notion, we found stronger selection on genes that would cause trans pleiotropic effects such as transcription factors (Supplementary file 1G).
evidence: GO enrichment analysis showing higher Vm/Vg for transcription factors

claim: There is limited evidence for genuine genetic variation for mutation rate.
source: There is limited evidence for genuine genetic variation for mutation rate.
evidence: General statement about the state of knowledge in the field

claim: Mutation rate is sensitive to environmental and physiological factors that cannot be easily controlled.
source: However, this is primarily due to technical limitations because mutation rate is sensitive to environmental and physiological factors that cannot be easily controlled and it is prohibitive to collect genetic data on mutation rates in natural populations.
evidence: Explanation for limited evidence of genetic variation in mutation rate

claim: The conclusions drawn in this study are likely to hold across genetic backgrounds, especially given the magnitude of apparent stabilizing selection.
source: Because of the close proximity of mutation rates in this study and earlier studies of the same species, the conclusions drawn in this study are likely to hold across genetic backgrounds, especially given the magnitude of apparent stabilizing selection, which is unlikely to be attributable to genetic factors unique to the ancestral line.
evidence: Inference from consistency with previous studies and magnitude of selection

claim: It is entirely possible that mutation rates may be different in inbred conditions than in natural populations.
source: It is entirely possible that mutation rates may be different in inbred conditions than in natural populations, which has significant theoretical consequences (Agrawal, 2002).
evidence: Acknowledgment of potential limitation, supported by citation to Agrawal, 2002

claim: The mutational variance observed in the MA lines appears to be too large (by a few orders of magnitude) to be solely explained by elevated mutation rates under stressful conditions.
source: While we could not formally exclude the possibility, the mutational variance we observed in the MA lines appears to be too large (by a few orders of magnitude) to be solely explained by elevated mutation rates under stressful conditions.
evidence: Inference from magnitude of observed mutational variance

claim: All MA lines were maintained in shell vials with 10 ml cornmeal-agar-molasses medium at 25°C, 70% humidity and 12 hr/12 hr light/dark cycle.
source: All lines were maintained in shell vials with 10 ml cornmeal-agar-molasses medium at 25°C, 70% humidity and 12 hr/12 hr light/dark cycle.
evidence: Description of experimental conditions

claim: Genomic DNA was extracted from 100 female flies per MA line at generation 60.
source: Genomic DNA was extracted from 100 female flies per MA line at generation 60 using the QIAGEN Genomic-tip 100/G kit (Qiagen, Valencia, CA).
evidence: Description of DNA extraction procedure

claim: Sequence data are deposited to the NCBI SRA database with the accession number for the BioProject SRP068116.
source: Sequence data are deposited to the NCBI SRA database with the accession number for the BioProject SRP068116.
evidence: Data availability statement

claim: 109,260,235 sites were considered where between 15 and 250 reads were observed in the parental line and in at least 10 MA lines.
source: We considered 109,260,235 sites where between 15 and 250 reads were observed in the parental line and in at least 10 MA lines, and no more than 10 possible alleles were observed in all lines combined.
